This duration is somewhat shorter than the 120 to 126 days reported in some general references, but it aligns well with empirical measurements taken under controlled laboratory conditions. The relatively long gestation for a rodent of this size likely reflects the energetic challenges of fetal development within a low-oxygen burrow system. Upon parturition, altricial neonates emerge weighing approximately 8 grams [Wwb = approximately 8 grams], a modest mass that underscores their dependence on maternal care and the substantial post-natal investment required. This neonatal mass represents a small fraction of the adult size, suggesting a strategy of producing relatively underdeveloped young that can be provisioned effectively in the safety of sealed nest chambers, where predation risk is minimal and microclimatic stability can be maintained throughout the critical early developmental period.

Following nutritional independence, the young disperse to establish their own burrow systems. This delayed reproductive maturity may be an adaptive response to the high costs of territory establishment and burrow excavation, which require a fully developed skeletal and muscular system.
